source.title: The Energy Cost of Reasoning: Analyzing Energy Usage in LLMs with Test-time Compute
source.authors: Yunho Jin; Gu-Yeon Wei; David Brooks

record.tranche_reason: The study compares benchmark accuracy across model sizes and reports a coding result where the 14B models perform worse than their 7B counterparts. It does not test pretraining-loss power laws, but its downstream-accuracy results qualify the claim that performance improves predictably with scale.
record.gate_note: The paper measures inference energy and task accuracy, not held-out cross-entropy loss, training tokens, or training compute. Its results on traditional model-size scaling and downstream benchmark accuracy bear on V6. Mentioned scaling-law sources and their findings are citations, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: The paper studies inference energy of test-time compute, but it reports benchmark accuracy across four off-the-shelf Qwen2.5 sizes (1.5B–32B). Those comparisons bear on V6, in an inference/TTC setting. They are incidental, use few points, fit no curve and involve no loss, so they are T3 rather than T5. Nothing bears on V1–V5 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record overstates the size anomaly. The authors mainly conclude that test-time compute generally gives better accuracy-energy trade-offs than increasing model size, with the largest gains on reasoning tasks and little gain on common-sense tasks. Indiscriminate TTC can raise energy by up to 113×. Output length tracks difficulty and correctness. The 14B-below-7B coding result is presented as a side anomaly: size alone does not guarantee accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: This is an inference-energy and benchmark-accuracy comparison across four Qwen2.5 sizes, with Base, majority-vote sampling, and reasoning-token configurations. It does not use the original studies' pretraining loss sweeps or scaling-law fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by task and inference configuration: coding accuracy is non-monotonic for the 7B-to-14B comparison in Base and MV, while the reported 1.5B-to-7B RT comparison on MATH500 improves.

fits_no_version.finding: Test-time compute (reasoning tokens) gives larger accuracy gains per unit inference energy than increasing model size. For example, RT 1.5B reaches 83.2% on MATH500 while Base 32B reaches 45.7%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time compute can substitute for parameter scaling in downstream accuracy at lower energy cost.

record.problems: The evidence relevant to V6 consists of selected comparisons and a stated coding anomaly, not a fitted predictive relationship. Numerical accuracy values are absent for the 14B-versus-7B coding anomaly. The study reports ten evaluation runs, but gives no uncertainty values for these accuracy comparisons in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were identified that directly test the listed versions. Most reported results compare TTC methods, energy consumption, output length, difficulty, or serving conditions rather than downstream scaling predictability.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss, token or compute sweeps; no power-law fits.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
No shape or architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes.
No functional fit of accuracy against scale or loss, and no prediction to unseen scales. Only four sizes of one off-the-shelf family are compared.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: RT 14B→32B on hard MATH500: marginal accuracy change for +0.6 Wh. RT 14B→32B on medium LiveCodeBench: a small gain (3.33%/Wh).
RT 32B vs RT 14B on LiveCodeBench: 14B gives up 7.8% accuracy for 1.74× less energy.
Base 32B scores only 45.7% on MATH500, and Base accuracy saturates at 48.3% (MATH500) and 23.5% (LiveCodeBench) across sizes.

record.verdict_notes: The models are released Qwen2.5 / R1-distill checkpoints, so size is confounded with other training differences. Accuracy is read mostly from figures, no uncertainty is given, and no scaling fit is attempted. The V6 evidence is weak and setting-specific.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law fitting and orders-of-magnitude ranges.
No fits on smaller runs or predictions for larger runs.
No fixed-compute training allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split.
No comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No power-law tests across modalities or training regimes.
The study reports task accuracy across model sizes, but does not fit or evaluate a predictive relationship with pretraining loss, and does not test extrapolation to unseen scales.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared Base model accuracy with Base 1.5B as model size increased.

conditions.value: mathematical benchmarks, averaged across four benchmarks

rows.locator: Section 4.1, Accuracy vs Energy per Query; Figure 1
rows.note: The paper reports the comparison as an aggregate across the mathematical benchmarks; it also describes the energy difference as negligible.
rows.check: Fine as a V6 row: a 4.8% gain from 1.5B to 7B, Base, math average (Fig. 1). The gain is small; the paper calls it 'only' 4.8%.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared Base model accuracy with Base 1.5B as model size increased.

conditions.value: coding benchmarks, averaged across four benchmarks

rows.measure: Accuracy and energy per query versus Base 1.5B
rows.value: 16.8% accuracy improvement; 40.1% lower energy consumption per query
rows.locator: Section 4.1, Accuracy vs Energy per Query; Figure 1
rows.note: Aggregate comparison across the coding benchmarks.
rows.check: Only the accuracy part (+16.8%) bears on V6. The 40.1% energy reduction is not a V6 measure and should be separated or noted as context.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 14B
rows.operation_detail: Compared Base model accuracy with Base 7B as model size increased.
rows.value: Base 14B has lower accuracy than its 7B counterpart; numerical value not stated
rows.note: The paper describes this as an anomaly and does not give the accuracy values in the text.
rows.check: The reversal is stated in text with no numbers. The models are off-the-shelf checkpoints, so size is not the only difference between them.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 14B
rows.operation_detail: Compared MV model accuracy with MV 7B as model size increased.
rows.value: MV 14B has lower accuracy than its 7B counterpart; numerical value not stated
rows.note: The paper reports the same 14B-below-7B anomaly for MV as for Base.
rows.check: Same as r3, for majority vote. MV is a TTC aggregation, so this is not plain model accuracy.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 7B
rows.stage_stated: reasoning-token configuration; model described as distilled from DeepSeek-R1
rows.operation_detail: Compared RT accuracy with the RT 1.5B model as model size increased.
rows.note: The paper says the 7B result approaches the performance of DeepSeek-R1, stated there as 617B parameters.
rows.check: The paper's text cites 'Figure 3(a)', but the values come from Figure 4(a), the MATH500 length sweep. The RT models are DeepSeek-R1 distills.

relationships.condition: 1.5B→7B Qwen2.5: Base on math and coding averages; RT on MATH500
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises with size in each case: +4.8% (r1), +16.8% (r2), and 83.2%→89.6% (r5).
relationships.display_finding: Base-model math and coding accuracy increased by 4.8% and 16.8%, respectively, while RT MATH500 accuracy increased from 83.2% to 89.6%.

relationships.reason: The paper explicitly states 14B accuracy is below 7B in both configurations (r3, r4). No numbers are given, and the checkpoints are not a controlled size sweep.
relationships.display_finding: The 14B model had lower accuracy than 7B in both configurations, although the checkpoints did not constitute a controlled size sweep.

relationships.condition: RT, 14B→32B, hard MATH500 and medium LiveCodeBench
relationships.reason: Per the text, not the rows: going to 32B has a 'marginal impact' on hard MATH500, and the medium LiveCodeBench gain is small (3.33%/Wh vs 39.5%/Wh). Gains with size flatten at the top of the range.
relationships.display_finding: Hard MATH500 showed only marginal improvement, and medium LiveCodeBench gains were small, with reported values of 3.33%/Wh versus 39.5%/Wh.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Base scaling from 1.5B to 7B on the reported aggregate math and coding benchmarks; RT scaling from 1.5B to 7B on MATH500
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy increases in these reported comparisons (r1, r2, r5), though the study does not establish predictability beyond the measured settings.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Coding benchmarks, Base and MV configurations, comparison of 7B and 14B models
reader_labels.reason: The paper explicitly reports lower accuracy for 14B than 7B in both configurations, contrary to a consistent improvement with scale (r3, r4).
